source.title: Memorizing without overfitting: Bias, variance, and interpolation in overparameterized models

record.file_problem: Full paper and supplemental material are present. The text includes flattened equations and figures, but is not cut off or garbled in a way that prevents reading the relevant findings.
record.tranche_reason: The authors analytically and numerically study interpolation and generalization in two simplified models, and explicitly qualify the broad claim: their models are convex and trained by ridge regression rather than stochastic gradient methods, and they do not test random labels or unstructured inputs. Their results refine the relationship between zero training error and overfitting rather than reproducing the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper's random-label, random-noise-image, and practical convolutional-network statements occur only as cited prior work in the Introduction. The paper's own experiments use teacher-generated labels, Gaussian input features, and ridge regression; it does not randomize labels or test shuffled or Gaussian-noise images. Rows below cover its own training-error, test-error, and bias/variance results relevant to interpolation and generalization.
record.test_reason: Random-label and random-noise-image fitting appear only as cited prior work. The study's own results concern teacher-generated regression labels, additive Gaussian label noise, and closed-form ridge regression in linear and fixed random-feature models. They do not test or specifically rebut V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors distinguish interpolation from overfitting and show that generalization can improve beyond interpolation in two convex regression models, without SGD and in the vanishing-regularization limit. They attribute the threshold divergence to variance and poorly sampled feature directions, and show that bias can produce overfitting without label noise. Their stated scope is fixed kernels and convex optimization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses analytic zero-temperature cavity calculations and numerical simulations of ridgeless ridge regression: linear regression and a two-layer random nonlinear features model with fixed random middle-layer weights and a trained top layer. Labels come from linear or nonlinear teacher models, not randomized image labels; there is no SGD training.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies with model type and ratios of features or parameters to data. Linear regression interpolates at αf = 1; the random nonlinear features model interpolates at αp = 1. Test error behavior also depends on αf relative to 1 in the random nonlinear features model. Bias differs between model types and depends on whether the teacher is linear or nonlinear.

fits_no_version.finding: Both ridge-regression models interpolate teacher-generated labels beyond their interpolation thresholds. Test error can improve with further model complexity; the linear model's behavior can be nonmonotonic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Interpolation and poor generalization are distinct in over-parameterized linear and fixed random-feature regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Variance causes the interpolation-threshold divergence, while bias remains finite; over-parameterized linear regression can have bias even when teacher and student match.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model architecture and incomplete sampling of feature space jointly determine bias and variance in over-parameterized regression.

fits_no_version.finding: At interpolation, linear regression overfits noisy linear-teacher labels and can also overfit noise-free nonlinear-teacher labels because of model mismatch.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model bias can produce overfitting without additive label noise.

record.problems: The paper studies only two simplified convex models in a fixed-feature or lazy setting, not practical deep networks trained with SGD. Its results use teacher-generated labels and do not directly test any claim version's random-label, unstructured-input, optimization-time, regularization, or learning-order condition. Numerical simulations use finite sample sizes, though the analysis is exact in a thermodynamic limit under a replica-symmetric assumption; the authors report small error bars and strong analytic-simulation agreement.
record.rows_left_out: No own-result rows omitted. Random-label fitting and random-noise image claims in the Introduction are attributed to cited Ref. [3] and are not this study's results.

untested.parts: All parts: standard deep networks trained by stochastic gradient methods on completely random labels, unchanged architecture and hyperparameters, near-zero training error and chance test performance.
Training-time comparison between true and random labels, and convergence versus label-corruption fraction.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs using the same networks. Gaussian covariates with teacher-dependent labels do not establish this.
A clean-to-fully-random label-corruption sweep, perfect training fit throughout, and test error rising toward chance.
Whether weight decay, dropout, and augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and whether removing them harms true-label generalization in the specified networks.
Training trajectories demonstrating shared real-data patterns learned before noisy or random labels.

record.verdict_notes: T5 is unwarranted: results about double descent do not qualify any specified random-label claim. All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V6; this does not deny the reported regression effects.

versions.untested_parts: No random labeling experiment; no stochastic gradient training; no standard deep-network architecture; no test error at chance under random labels.
No comparison of training time for random versus true labels and no label-corruption sweep.
No shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input fitting experiment.
No sweep from clean to fully randomized labels or corresponding test-error curve.
No random-label test of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation, nor comparison of their removal on true-label generalization.
No training trajectory comparing learning of real-label patterns with noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: linear regression (no basis functions)
rows.size_stated: M = 512 data points in numerical simulations; Nf = Np; ratios varied
rows.operation_detail: Ridgeless-limit ridge regression fit to teacher-generated labels; training error reported as a function of feature-to-data ratio αf.

conditions.value: λ = 10⁻⁶ in simulations; analytic results in λ → 0 limit

rows.value: Below αf = 1, training error is finite and decreases monotonically; at αf = 1 it reaches zero; beyond the threshold it remains pinned at zero.
rows.uncertainty: Small error bars indicate error on the mean; plotted points averaged over 1000 independent simulations except at phase transition, where each point is averaged over 150000 simulations.
rows.locator: Sec. IV B; Fig. 2(a); Supplemental Material Sec. S4 A
rows.note: This is interpolation on teacher-generated labels, not randomized labels. Numerical simulations use M = M′ = 512, signal-to-noise ratio 10, and λ = 10⁻⁶.
rows.check: Interpolation of teacher-generated regression labels does not measure any version's effect. Zero error is an analytic ridgeless-limit result; finite-λ simulations approximate it.

rows.subject: linear regression (no basis functions)
rows.size_stated: M = 512 data points in numerical simulations; Nf = Np; ratios varied
rows.operation_detail: Test error measured as feature-to-data ratio αf crosses the interpolation threshold.

conditions.value: λ = 10⁻⁶ in simulations; analytic results in λ → 0 limit

rows.value: Test error diverges at αf = 1; for αf > 1, it decreases with αf.
rows.uncertainty: Small error bars indicate error on the mean; plotted points averaged over 1000 independent simulations except at phase transition, where each point is averaged over 150000 simulations.
rows.note: Generalization is measured on new data from the same teacher distribution, not on a random-label test set.
rows.check: Teacher-distribution regression test error does not measure any version. The blanket assertion that test error decreases for all αf > 1 needs qualification: the summary of major results explicitly describes nonmonotonic behavior, consistent with Eq. (28).

rows.subject: linear regression (no basis functions)
rows.size_stated: M = 512 data points in numerical simulations; Nf = Np; ratios varied
rows.operation_detail: Bias and variance measured across feature-to-data ratios in ridgeless regression.
rows.value: For αf ≤ 1, bias is zero; variance diverges at the interpolation threshold. For αf > 1, variance decreases monotonically while bias increases monotonically.
rows.note: These findings describe the paper's standard labels and model, not the V4 random-label corruption sweep.
rows.check: Bias and variance across model complexity do not measure any version. The stated monotonic variance decrease follows the prose, but Eq. (30) contains a signal contribution proportional to (αf−1)/αf²; monotonicity is not unconditional across noise settings.

rows.subject: random nonlinear features model (two-layer neural network; random fixed middle-layer weights; trained top layer)
rows.size_stated: M = 512 data points in numerical simulations; Np and Nf varied
rows.operation_detail: Ridgeless-limit ridge regression fit to teacher-generated labels using ReLU random nonlinear features.

conditions.value: λ = 10⁻⁶ in simulations; analytic results in λ → 0 limit
αp = Np/M and αf = Nf/M varied

rows.value: Training error is finite when αp < 1 and goes to zero when αp ≥ 1.
rows.uncertainty: Small error bars indicate error on the mean; plotted points averaged over 1000 independent simulations except at phase transition, where each point is averaged over 150000 simulations.
rows.locator: Sec. IV C; Fig. 3(a), (c); Supplemental Material Sec. S4 A
rows.note: This is a simplified two-layer model with a fixed random hidden layer; it does not use stochastic gradient descent or random labels.
rows.check: The model interpolates teacher-generated labels by fitting its output layer through ridge regression; this does not establish random-label or unstructured-input fitting by the networks and training procedure named in the versions.

rows.subject: random nonlinear features model (two-layer neural network; random fixed middle-layer weights; trained top layer)
rows.size_stated: M = 512 data points in numerical simulations; Np and Nf varied
rows.operation_detail: Test error measured across parameter-to-data and feature-to-data ratios.

conditions.value: λ = 10⁻⁶ in simulations; analytic results in λ → 0 limit

rows.value: Test error diverges along the interpolation boundary αp = 1; for αf < 1 it shows canonical double-descent behavior.
rows.uncertainty: Small error bars indicate error on the mean; plotted points averaged over 1000 independent simulations except at phase transition, where each point is averaged over 150000 simulations.
rows.note: Test data are drawn from the same teacher distribution; the paper does not measure chance error on randomized labels.
rows.check: Double descent across parameter counts on teacher-generated regression data does not measure a label-corruption sweep or any other version.

rows.subject: random nonlinear features model (two-layer neural network; random fixed middle-layer weights; trained top layer)
rows.size_stated: M = 512 data points in numerical simulations; Np and Nf varied
rows.operation_detail: Bias and variance measured across parameter-to-data and feature-to-data ratios.
rows.value: Bias remains finite and decreases monotonically for all αp; variance accounts for the test-error divergence at phase boundaries.
rows.note: The authors report bias never reaches zero for this nonlinear-feature model, even with a linear teacher.
rows.check: Bias and variance decomposition in a fixed random-feature model does not measure any version.

rows.subject: linear regression (no basis functions)
rows.size_stated: M = 512 data points in numerical simulations; Nf = Np; ratios varied
rows.operation_detail: Fit to labels from a nonlinear tanh teacher, with and without additive label noise, at the interpolation threshold.
rows.measure: Qualitative fit/generalization behavior along the minimum principal component; authors state the model overfits in the absence of label noise when biased.
rows.baseline: Linear teacher without label noise: model avoids overfitting and approximates the true relationship.
rows.value: With nonlinear teacher and no label noise, the model still overfits the training data.
rows.locator: Sec. V C; Fig. 5(d), (f); Supplemental Material Sec. S4 B, D
rows.note: An own-result refinement about bias and overfitting; it does not test fitting randomly labeled images.
rows.check: Noise-free overfitting from teacher–student mismatch does not measure any version. The scatter plots use M = M′ = 200, not 512 (Supplement Sec. S4 D). The nonlinear-teacher comparison is Fig. 5(e),(f); Fig. 5(d) is the linear-teacher noise-free control.

rows.subject: linear regression (no basis functions)
rows.size_stated: M = 512 data points in numerical simulations; Nf = Np; ratios varied
rows.operation_detail: Fit to labels from a linear teacher, with and without additive label noise, at the interpolation threshold.
rows.measure: Qualitative fit/generalization behavior along the minimum principal component
rows.baseline: Linear teacher without label noise: model avoids overfitting and approximates the true relationship.
rows.value: With label noise, the model overfits the training data and the learned slope does not accurately reflect the true relationship.
rows.locator: Sec. V C; Fig. 5(c), (d); Supplemental Material Sec. S4 B, D
rows.note: This result is about conventional label noise in the paper's regression setup.
rows.check: Overfitting additive Gaussian regression noise does not measure random-label fitting or learning order. These scatter plots use M = M′ = 200, not 512 (Supplement Sec. S4 D).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
